question: A downloaded file is named "Invoice_40218.pdf.exe". What's the biggest red flag here?

options.text: The filename is too long
The real file extension is .exe (a program), not .pdf
It has numbers in the name
It was sent as an email attachment

explanation: The ".pdf" is just part of the filename — the actual, working extension is ".exe", meaning double-clicking it runs a program instead of opening a document. Many file browsers hide known extensions by default, making this easy to miss.

question: Before encrypting any files, what does ransomware typically do first?

options.text: Immediately show the ransom note
Quietly disable backups and shadow copies
Email all of your contacts
Restart the computer

explanation: Disabling built-in backup and recovery features first, before doing anything visible, means there's nothing easy to restore from once the ransom note finally appears.

question: Why is a shared network drive especially dangerous during a ransomware infection?

options.text: It makes files load more slowly
One infected computer can encrypt files on every computer sharing that drive
It uses more storage space
It requires an extra password

explanation: Ransomware actively scans for reachable network shares to spread to — a single infected laptop can lock files across an entire office, not just its own hard drive.

question: Should you pay the ransom to get your files back?

options.text: Yes, always — it's the fastest way to recover
No — there's no guarantee of a working key, and it funds further attacks
Only if the amount is small
Yes, but only using a credit card

explanation: Paying doesn't guarantee the attacker actually sends a working decryption key, confirms the business is willing to pay (inviting repeat attacks), and directly funds the attacker's next target.

question: What's the single most effective protection against ransomware?

options.text: A strong antivirus program alone
An offline backup that ransomware on the network can't also reach
A very long password
Permanently disabling internet access

explanation: A backup that's also connected to the network can get encrypted right along with everything else — a real backup needs to be kept offline or otherwise disconnected so ransomware can't reach it too.
